rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This run will establish the elution window and critical pairs for subsequent slope and temperature adjustments.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient to test whether full resolution can be maintained with faster elution, using the substantial resolution margin.
Shorten the gradient another grid step while holding composition and temperature fixed. The current minimum resolution of 2.54 leaves room to reduce elution time while preserving the maximum CRF.
Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The first pair may fall below 1.5; injection 3 remains the fastest demonstrated method achieving maximum CRF.
Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test faster elution and temperature-dependent selectivity. The first pair is the key constraint, with resolution 1.73 at 40 C.

Cooling should improve the critical early pair’s selectivity, while lowering phi1 makes the two-minute gradient shallower. Test whether these changes recover full resolution with faster elution than injection 3; the final hold should still elute the last compound comfortably within 42 minutes.

Increase the final organic fraction one step to accelerate the last peak while retaining the favorable low-temperature selectivity. This tests whether the critical first pair’s resolution margin of 1.59 is sufficient for a slightly steeper gradient.

Raise phi0 one step to reduce the gradient span while keeping the stronger final eluent that accelerated the last peak. Test whether the shallower slope restores the first pair to R ≥ 1.5 without losing the time advantage.

Shift both endpoints upward one grid step, preserving the slope that fully resolved injection 8 while strengthening the final hold. This should accelerate the last peak; monitor the first pair for compression from the stronger starting eluent.

Shift both endpoints upward another step, preserving the successful gradient slope and reaching the strongest available final eluent. Test whether this further shortens elution while maintaining the first pair’s resolution above 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while retaining the minimum gradient duration and strongest final eluent. This tests faster elution with a shallower gradient, while checking whether the earliest pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

Raise temperature one grid step to accelerate the last peak while using injection 11’s improved first-pair resolution margin. This checks whether modest heating preserves maximum CRF at the two-minute gradient.

Increase phi0 one step to test further acceleration and a shallower gradient at 30 C. The earliest peak is now near the pre-gradient outlet window, so this run will determine whether stronger starting solvent compromises the critical first pair.

Back off the starting organic fraction to 0.30 and test the next temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This brackets the heating limit for the critical first pair; injection 12 remains the speed benchmark at maximum CRF.

Narrow the gradient span to recover the first pair’s resolution at 35 C, targeting R just above 1.5. This tests an alternative maximum-CRF method, although the weaker final hold may delay the last peak relative to injection 12.

Lower phi0 to retain the earliest pair longer, since reducing the slope alone barely improved its resolution near the dead-time region. Test whether this restores full resolution at 35 C; injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Reduce phi1 one grid step to make the gradient shallower, targeting recovery of the first pair from R 1.42 to at least 1.5. This explores a fully resolved alternative at 35 C while retaining injection 12 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Refine around injection 12, the fastest clearly fully resolved method, by lowering phi1 one step to test additional resolution margin at modest time cost. Injection 17’s first pair is still flagged below threshold despite rounding to 1.50, so it is not a confirmed fully resolved alternative.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 18 to move the earliest peaks away from the dead-time region while testing whether full resolution survives the steeper slope. This characterizes a nearby maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether cooling restores the early-pair resolution lost at phi0 0.35 and 30 C. This closes the remaining nearby starting-composition boundary, while injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Back off phi0 from the failed 0.35 condition and test a slightly shallower gradient at 25 C for additional resolution margin. This characterizes a nearby, potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative while retaining injection 12 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the remaining lower-phi0 neighbor of injection 12 with the strongest final eluent. This brackets whether moving the early peaks farther from the dead-time region can preserve full resolution without the slower final hold used in injection 19.

Cool injection 19 by one grid step to improve its marginal first-pair resolution while keeping the early peaks away from the dead-time region. This tests a nearby maximum-CRF alternative with more resolution margin; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Reduce phi1 one step from injection 19 to improve the first pair’s narrow resolution margin while retaining a two-minute gradient. This refines a nearby maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the remaining nearby shallower-gradient condition for additional resolution margin while preserving maximum CRF. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
